stage_description: The senior stage begins at roughly one to one-and-a-half years. The hamster shows the first signs of age: it runs less on the wheel, sleeps more, and moves less briskly. The risk of age-related disease rises — tumors (common in hamsters), heart and kidney problems, and dental issues — and the coat may thin. The goal of care is to catch problems early and keep the animal comfortable.
nutrition: Keep the familiar complete food, but watch the weight, since both weight loss and obesity are undesirable. An older hamster may find it easier to eat slightly softened food and soft pieces of vegetable if its teeth or gums bother it. Fresh water should always be within easy reach, with the bottle placed low.
activity: Leave the wheel and burrowing options in place, but do not force the hamster to be active. Lower the platforms and cage levels and use softer bedding to reduce the risk of falls and injury. More hideouts and a calm environment help an aging pet feel secure.
veterinary_check_frequency: Exams with an exotics veterinarian are best done about every six months so age-related changes are caught in good time. At home, weigh your hamster regularly and gently feel for lumps so that tumors can be found at an early stage.
dental_care: Teeth and gums need more attention with age. Keep offering safe things to gnaw and watch the appetite: if the hamster drops food, eats slowly, or loses weight, overgrown or diseased teeth may be the cause and should be examined by a veterinarian.
warning_signs: Watch for noticeable weight loss, reduced activity, a ruffled or thinning coat, palpable lumps, labored breathing, and increased thirst and urination. Any of these is a reason to have your hamster seen by a veterinarian without delay.
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and does not replace consultation with a veterinarian.
